title: Stoichiometry: the mole, balanced equations, limiting reactants and percent yield
summary: Students learn to count particles with the mole, balance chemical equations and use mole ratios to predict amounts of products. They apply limiting reactants and percent yield in two labs: baking soda and vinegar, and copper chloride and aluminum foil.
brief: Stoichiometry for grade 10 chemistry: ten 55-minute lessons on the mole, molar mass, balancing equations, mole ratios, limiting reactants and percent yield. Two labs: a baking soda and vinegar reaction to find the mass of carbon dioxide released, and a copper chloride and aluminum foil reaction to find the limiting reactant, each with a lab report. Problem sets twice a week. Grading: lab reports 30%, problem sets 20%, unit test 50%.
policies:
Goggles, apron and closed-toe shoes are required on lab days; a student without them observes and writes up the data from a partner. No food or drink in the lab.

Problem sets are due at the start of class two days after they are set. Late sets lose 10% a day, up to three days.

Lab reports are written individually from data collected with a partner; shared data is fine, shared wording is not.

Bring a scientific calculator and a periodic table every day. The unit test allows both.

segments.title: The mole as a counting unit
segments.description:
Compare the dozen and the pair with the mole, then state 1 mol = 6.022 × 10²³ particles.
Before the reveal, students predict whether 2.50 mol of water molecules is more or fewer than 6.022 × 10²³ and write the calculation they would use.
Work it through: 2.50 mol × 6.022 × 10²³ molecules/mol = 1.51 × 10²⁴ molecules.
Then reverse it: 3.01 × 10²³ atoms of Cu ÷ 6.022 × 10²³ atoms/mol = 0.500 mol.
segments.teacherNotes: Misconception: the mole is a mass. It is a number, like a dozen. Say ‘particles’ for atoms, molecules or formula units. Give scale: one mole of water is about 18 g, roughly a tablespoon.

segments.title: Moles and particles practice
segments.description:
Students work the three items alone, writing each answer with its unit.
Partners compare answers for one minute, then check the class answers.
Circulate and look for a multiply versus divide mix-up.
segments.teacherNotes:
Items and answers:
(a) 0.250 mol CO₂ to molecules: 1.51 × 10²³
(b) 1.806 × 10²⁴ molecules H₂O to moles: 3.00 mol
(c) 4.00 mol Cu to atoms: 2.41 × 10²⁴
Tip: more moles means more particles, so check the size of each answer.

segments.title: Molar mass from the periodic table
segments.description:
Define molar mass as the mass of 1 mol in g/mol. Work out CO₂ on the board: 1 C + 2 O = 12.01 + 2(16.00) = 44.01 g/mol.
Students calculate CuCl₂ alone using the atomic masses on the screen, then check with a partner.
Work out NaHCO₃ together, counting each atom: Na, H, C and three O.
segments.teacherNotes: Answers: CuCl₂ = 63.55 + 2(35.45) = 134.45 g/mol. NaHCO₃ = 22.99 + 1.01 + 12.01 + 3(16.00) = 84.01 g/mol. Common mistake: ignoring a subscript. Use atomic masses to two decimals.

Your turn: find the molar mass of CuCl₂.

segments.title: Converting between grams and moles
segments.description:
Show the two forms: moles = grams ÷ molar mass, and grams = moles × molar mass.
Work one example: 22.0 g CO₂ ÷ 44.01 g/mol = 0.500 mol.
Students then work 2.00 mol NaHCO₃ to grams on their own and show the units cancelling.
Check the answer on the board.
segments.teacherNotes: Answer: 2.00 mol × 84.01 g/mol = 168 g. Tip: write molar mass as a fraction so that the unit you want ends up on top and the other unit cancels.
shown: Table: Going from | To | Do this / grams | moles | divide by molar mass / moles | grams | multiply by molar mass
Your turn: What is the mass of 2.00 mol of NaHCO₃?

segments.title: Grams and moles practice
segments.description:
Students work the two items alone, one step each, using the molar masses given with them.
They spend about one minute on each item.
Partners check answers for one minute.
Go over only an item the class disagrees on.
segments.teacherNotes:
Molar masses given: CO₂ 44.01 g/mol, NaHCO₃ 84.01 g/mol.
Items and answers:
(a) 88.02 g CO₂ to moles: 2.00 mol
(b) 0.500 mol NaHCO₃ to grams: 42.0 g
Keep the pace: one calculation per item. If a student gets stuck, ask which unit must end up on top.

segments.title: Find and fix the mistake
segments.description:
Give out the sheet “Find and fix the mistake”.
The sheet has a student’s worked solution. Each student writes what went wrong and redoes the work correctly.

Hear two explanations and the corrected answer.
segments.teacherNotes: Mistake: the subscript 2 on Cl was ignored, so the molar mass should be 63.55 + 2(35.45) = 134.45 g/mol. Correct answer: 13.4 g ÷ 134.45 g/mol = 0.0997 mol. The student’s 0.135 mol is too large, which the molar mass would have shown.

keyIdeas: A mole is 6.022 × 10²³ particles (Avogadro’s number), a counting unit like a dozen but far larger, used because atoms and molecules are far too small to count one by one.
To convert between moles and particles, multiply by 6.022 × 10²³ to go from moles to particles and divide by it to go back.
Molar mass is the mass of one mole of a substance in g/mol. You find it by adding the atomic masses from the periodic table, counting every atom shown by a subscript.
Molar mass links grams to moles: moles = grams ÷ molar mass, and grams = moles × molar mass.

vocabulary.definition: The SI unit for an amount of substance: 6.022 × 10²³ particles.
6.022 × 10²³, the number of particles in one mole.
A single atom, molecule or formula unit of a substance.
A group of atoms joined by covalent bonds, such as CO₂ or H₂O.
The smallest whole-number ratio of ions in an ionic compound, such as NaHCO₃ or CuCl₂.
The average mass of an atom of an element, found on the periodic table; in g/mol it is the mass of one mole of atoms.
The mass in grams of one mole of a substance, in g/mol, found by adding the atomic masses of all atoms in its formula.
A ratio equal to 1 used to change units, such as 44.01 g CO₂ / 1 mol CO₂.

study.overview: Atoms and molecules are far too small to count one by one, so chemists count them in moles. A mole is a number of particles, 6.022 × 10²³ of them, and it works the way a dozen does. Molar mass then links the mass you can weigh on a balance to the number of moles you want. This guide covers the mole, converting between moles and particles, finding molar mass from the periodic table, and converting between grams and moles.

points.heading: The mole is a number, not a mass
points.explanation: A dozen is 12 items and a pair is 2 items. A mole is 6.022 × 10²³ items, a number known as Avogadro’s number. We use the word particles for atoms, molecules or formula units. Nuts in a hardware store are counted by weighing, and chemists do the same with tiny particles. A mole is not a mass, but it does have a convenient size: one mole of water has a mass of about 18 g, roughly a tablespoon. Always read 1 mol as 6.022 × 10²³ particles of whatever substance is named.

points.heading: Converting between moles and particles
points.explanation: Multiply by 6.022 × 10²³ to go from moles to particles. Divide by 6.022 × 10²³ to go from particles to moles. Example: how many molecules are in 2.50 mol of water? 2.50 mol × 6.022 × 10²³ molecules/mol = 1.51 × 10²⁴ molecules. Now reverse it: 3.01 × 10²³ atoms of Cu ÷ 6.022 × 10²³ atoms/mol = 0.500 mol. Check the size of every answer. More moles must mean more particles, so a sample of 2.50 mol has more than 6.022 × 10²³ molecules, and half of that number of atoms is half a mole. If your answer goes the wrong way, you probably multiplied when you should have divided, or the reverse.

points.heading: Molar mass comes from the periodic table
points.explanation: Molar mass is the mass of one mole of a substance, in g/mol. Add the atomic masses of every atom in the formula, and count each atom shown by a subscript. Use two decimal places. Example with CO₂: it has 1 C and 2 O, so 12.01 + 2(16.00) = 44.01 g/mol. Example with NaCl: it has 1 Na and 1 Cl, so 22.99 + 35.45 = 58.44 g/mol. Example with water: it has 2 H and 1 O, so 2(1.01) + 16.00 = 18.02 g/mol. The most common mistake is ignoring a subscript, so write out how many atoms of each element you have before you add.

points.heading: Converting between grams and moles
points.explanation: Molar mass is the bridge between grams and moles. To go from grams to moles, divide by the molar mass: moles = grams ÷ molar mass. To go from moles to grams, multiply: grams = moles × molar mass. Write the molar mass as a fraction so the unit you want sits on top and the other unit cancels. Example: 22.0 g of CO₂ ÷ 44.01 g/mol = 0.500 mol. Example: the mass of 3.00 mol of water is 3.00 mol × 18.02 g/mol = 54.1 g, and the mol units cancel. To go from grams to particles, take two steps: first find moles by dividing by molar mass, then multiply by 6.022 × 10²³. For 9.01 g of water, 9.01 g ÷ 18.02 g/mol = 0.500 mol, and 0.500 mol × 6.022 × 10²³ molecules/mol = 3.01 × 10²³ molecules.

handouts.title: Moles and particles practice

blocks.text: Work each item alone. Write each answer with its unit. Use 1 mol = 6.022 × 10²³ particles.
(a) Convert 0.250 mol CO₂ to molecules.

blocks.hint: Answer with unit

blocks.text: (b) Convert 1.806 × 10²⁴ molecules H₂O to moles.

blocks.hint: Answer with unit

blocks.text: (c) Convert 4.00 mol Cu to atoms.

blocks.hint: Answer with unit

handouts.key:
(a) 0.250 mol × 6.022 × 10²³ molecules/mol = 1.5055 × 10²³ molecules ≈ 1.51 × 10²³ molecules of CO₂.
(b) 1.806 × 10²⁴ molecules ÷ (6.022 × 10²³ molecules/mol) = 2.998… mol ≈ 3.00 mol H₂O.
(c) 4.00 mol × 6.022 × 10²³ atoms/mol = 2.4088 × 10²⁴ atoms ≈ 2.41 × 10²⁴ atoms of Cu.
Look for multiplication when converting moles to particles and division when converting particles to moles. Common slips: reversing these operations, mishandling powers of ten, or labeling Cu particles as molecules instead of atoms.

handouts.title: Grams and moles practice

blocks.text: Work each item alone, in one step. Write the answer with its unit.

items: Molar mass of CO₂: 44.01 g/mol
Molar mass of NaHCO₃: 84.01 g/mol

blocks.text: (a) Convert 88.02 g CO₂ to moles.

blocks.hint: Answer with unit

blocks.text: (b) Convert 0.500 mol NaHCO₃ to grams.

blocks.hint: Answer with unit

handouts.key:
(a) 88.02 g ÷ 44.01 g/mol = 2.00 mol CO₂. Accept 2.000 mol, which retains four significant figures.
(b) 0.500 mol × 84.01 g/mol = 42.005 g ≈ 42.0 g NaHCO₃.
Look for units that cancel to leave mol in (a) and g in (b). Common slip: multiplying by molar mass in (a) or dividing by it in (b).

handouts.title: Find and fix the mistake

blocks.text: A student was asked: how many moles are in 13.4 g of CuCl₂? Here is the student's worked solution. Atomic masses: Cu 63.55, Cl 35.45.
The student's work

items: Molar mass of CuCl₂ = 63.55 + 35.45 = 99.00 g/mol
Moles = 13.4 g ÷ 99.00 g/mol
Moles = 0.135 mol

blocks.text: 1. Write what went wrong.

blocks.hint: One or two sentences

blocks.text: 2. Redo the work correctly. Show the molar mass, the division and the units.

blocks.hint: Corrected work and final answer with unit

handouts.key:
1. The student counted only one chlorine atom. The subscript 2 in CuCl₂ means two chlorine atoms per formula unit, so chlorine's atomic mass must be multiplied by 2. The molar mass is too small, making the calculated number of moles too large.
2. Molar mass of CuCl₂ = 63.55 + 2(35.45) = 134.45 g/mol.
Moles = 13.4 g ÷ 134.45 g/mol = 0.099665… mol ≈ 0.0997 mol CuCl₂.
Look for the factor of 2 on chlorine, division by the corrected molar mass, and a final unit of mol. Common slip: multiplying the copper contribution by 2 as well.

handouts.title: Exit slip

blocks.text: Finish this sentence in writing.
To go from grams to particles, I first...

blocks.hint: Finish the sentence

handouts.key:
Expected completion: Divide the mass in grams by the molar mass to find moles, then multiply the moles by 6.022 × 10²³ particles/mol.
Accept equivalent wording that gives both operations in this order. Look for a clear distinction between molar mass and the number of particles per mole. Common slip: multiplying grams directly by 6.022 × 10²³ without first converting to moles.

segments.title: Do the atoms add up?
segments.description:
Tell students that Problem sets: The mole, Avogadro’s number and molar mass is due now.
Put the unbalanced equation on the screen. Each student counts the O atoms on each side and writes “can be right” or “cannot be right” with a few words of reason.
Partners compare for one minute, then hear one answer.
segments.teacherNotes: Answer: 2 O on the left and 1 O on the right, so an oxygen atom would vanish. Hydrogen already matches, with 2 H on each side. Link: last time students counted particles in moles; now they count atoms on each side of an arrow.
shown: H₂ + O₂ → H₂O
Count the O atoms on each side. Can this equation be right? Write a few words of reason.

segments.title: Coefficients and subscripts
segments.description:
Name the reactants, the products and the arrow, and state that atoms are neither created nor destroyed.
Separate the coefficient from the subscript using H₂O.
Students write which number they would change to fix the oxygen in H₂ + O₂ → H₂O, and why, then tell a partner.
Balance it together: a 2 in front of H₂O, then a 2 in front of H₂, then recount every element.
segments.teacherNotes: Answer: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, with 4 H and 2 O on each side. Misconception: changing H₂O to H₂O₂ looks like a fix, but H₂O₂ is hydrogen peroxide, a different substance. Only coefficients change.
shown: Side by side: Coefficient: written in front of a formula; multiplies every atom in it; this is what we change | Subscript: written low after a symbol; part of the substance’s identity; never changed
Which number could you change to fix the oxygen in H₂ + O₂ → H₂O? Write your choice and one reason.

segments.title: A method for balancing
segments.description:
Put the steps on the screen and work Fe + O₂ → Fe₂O₃ with the class.
Count atoms, then stop at oxygen: 2 on the left and 3 on the right.
Students predict the smallest number of oxygen atoms both sides can reach, and tell a partner.
Finish together: 2Fe₂O₃ first (the only compound), then the single elements 3O₂ and 4Fe, then recount.
segments.teacherNotes: Answer: both sides reach 6 O, so 3O₂ and 2Fe₂O₃. Then Fe on the right is 4, so 4Fe + 3O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃. Tip: leave a lone element, such as Fe or O₂, until last, since changing it disturbs nothing else.
shown: Steps: count atoms of each element → pick an element and make both sides equal → leave single-element substances for last → recount every element
Fe + O₂ → Fe₂O₃

segments.title: Balance three equations
segments.description:
Students balance three equations alone, writing an atom count for each.
Partners compare and settle any difference by recounting.
Check the answers on the board, taking the aluminum and copper chloride equation last.
segments.teacherNotes:
Items and answers:

study.overview: A balanced chemical equation shows that atoms are neither created nor destroyed in a reaction, so each element has the same number of atoms on both sides of the arrow. You balance an equation by changing coefficients only. Once it is balanced, the coefficients give mole ratios, and you can use those ratios as conversion factors to find how many moles of one substance react or form from a known amount of another.

points.heading: Balanced means the same atoms on both sides
points.explanation: Atoms are rearranged in a reaction, never lost or made. So every element must be counted equally on the left and the right. Take H₂ + O₂ → H₂O. The left side has 2 O atoms and the right side has 1 O atom, so an oxygen atom would vanish. The equation cannot be right as written. The balanced version, 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, has 4 H and 2 O on each side. Always recount every element at the end, not only the one you were fixing.

points.heading: Change coefficients, never subscripts
points.explanation: A coefficient is the number in front of a formula, and it multiplies every atom in that formula. A subscript is the small number after a symbol, and it is part of the substance’s identity. Changing H₂O to H₂O₂ might seem to fix the oxygen, but H₂O₂ is hydrogen peroxide, a different substance. So only coefficients change. A method that works: count the atoms of each element, pick one element and make both sides equal, leave single-element substances such as Fe or O₂ for last, then recount. For Fe + O₂ → Fe₂O₃, oxygen is 2 on the left and 3 on the right. Fe₂O₃ is the only compound, so change it first: 2Fe₂O₃ gives 6 O, a number O₂ can match. Then fix the single elements last: 3O₂ gives 6 O on the left. Now the right side has 4 Fe, so write 4Fe. The result is 4Fe + 3O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃.

points.heading: Coefficients are mole ratios, not mass ratios
points.explanation: In 2Al + 3CuCl₂ → 2AlCl₃ + 3Cu, the coefficients mean that 2 mol Al react with 3 mol CuCl₂ to make 2 mol AlCl₃ and 3 mol Cu. They do not describe grams. The masses of those moles are 2 mol Al = 53.96 g and 3 mol CuCl₂ = 403.35 g, which are not in a 2 : 3 ratio. To compare amounts in a reaction, convert to moles first. Any two substances in the equation give a mole ratio. For CuCl₂ and AlCl₃ it is 3 mol CuCl₂ / 2 mol AlCl₃.

points.heading: Use the mole ratio as a conversion factor
points.explanation: A mole ratio is a fraction with units. Put the substance you want on top and the substance you have on the bottom, so the units you have cancel. Suppose 4.00 mol Al react completely in the equation above. Then 4.00 mol Al × (3 mol Cu / 2 mol Al) = 6.00 mol Cu, and mol Al cancels. You can turn the problem around too. Suppose 9.00 mol Cu form and you want the Al used. The wanted substance goes on top: 9.00 mol Cu × (2 mol Al / 3 mol Cu) = 6.00 mol Al. Check that the answer makes sense. The equation has a smaller coefficient for Al (2) than for Cu (3), so fewer moles of Al than Cu should be involved.

handouts.title: Balance three equations

blocks.text: Balance each equation by changing coefficients only. Under each one, write an atom count for every element, left side and right side.
(a) Mg + O₂ → MgO

blocks.hint: Your balanced equation, then the atom count on each side

blocks.text: (b) C₃H₈ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O

blocks.hint: Your balanced equation, then the atom count on each side

blocks.text: (c) Al + CuCl₂ → AlCl₃ + Cu

blocks.hint: Your balanced equation, then the atom count on each side

handouts.key:
(a) 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. Atom counts: Mg—left 2, right 2; O—left 2, right 2. Look for the smallest whole-number coefficients, 2 : 1 : 2. Common slip: changing MgO to MgO₂ instead of changing coefficients.

(b) C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O. Atom counts: C—left 3, right 3; H—left 8, right 8; O—left 10, right 10. The products contain 3 × 2 + 4 × 1 = 10 oxygen atoms, requiring 5O₂. Common slip: counting only the oxygen in CO₂ and overlooking the oxygen in H₂O.

(c) 2Al + 3CuCl₂ → 2AlCl₃ + 3Cu. Atom counts: Al—left 2, right 2; Cu—left 3, right 3; Cl—left 6, right 6. Common slip: balancing chlorine but forgetting to adjust aluminum or copper.

For all equations, accept whole-number multiples that balance every element, while encouraging the smallest whole-number coefficients. Formulas and subscripts must stay unchanged.

Write the mole ratio of H₂ to NH₃.

blocks.text: Write the mole ratio of N₂ to NH₃.

blocks.hint: Ratio with units

blocks.hint: Calculation and answer

blocks.text: The same reaction makes 8.0 mol NH₃. How many moles of N₂ were used? Show your calculation with units.

blocks.hint: Calculation and answer

handouts.key:
1. Mole ratio of H₂ to NH₃: 3 mol H₂ / 2 mol NH₃. Common slip: reversing the requested ratio.

2. Mole ratio of N₂ to NH₃: 1 mol N₂ / 2 mol NH₃. Look for recognition that N₂ has an implied coefficient of 1. Common slip: using the subscript 2 as its coefficient.

3. 8.0 mol NH₃ × (3 mol H₂ / 2 mol NH₃) = 12 mol H₂. Look for cancellation of mol NH₃ and a final unit of mol H₂. The answer has two significant figures. Common slip: multiplying by 2/3 instead of 3/2.

4. 8.0 mol NH₃ × (1 mol N₂ / 2 mol NH₃) = 4.0 mol N₂. Look for cancellation of mol NH₃ and a final unit of mol N₂. The answer has two significant figures. Common slip: multiplying by 2 instead of 1/2.

The coefficients in a balanced equation tell me...

Expected completion: The coefficients in a balanced equation tell me the relative numbers of moles of each substance that react or form.

Accept wording that identifies a fixed mole ratio between substances. A response may also correctly describe relative numbers of particles, such as molecules or formula units. Look for the idea of relative amounts rather than a required batch size. Common slips: saying coefficients give gram ratios or confusing coefficients with the numbers of atoms within a formula.

keyIdeas: Mass-to-mass problems follow one path: grams of what you have → moles of what you have → moles of what you want (using the mole ratio) → grams of what you want. The mole ratio is the only step that uses the balanced equation.
The limiting reactant is the one that runs out first and sets how much product can form. To find it, compare the moles you have with the moles the reaction needs. Do not compare grams.
The excess reactant is the one left over. Find the moles it used by following the limiting reactant, subtract from the moles you started with, then convert to grams.
Grams do not follow the coefficients. A reactant with a smaller mass can still be in excess, because molar masses differ.

study.overview: Stoichiometry questions in grams all follow one route. You convert grams to moles, use the balanced equation to switch substances, then convert back to grams. When two reactants are given, one runs out first and sets how much product forms. This guide shows the route, how to find the limiting reactant, how to find what is left over, and why grams can mislead you. Keep your periodic table and calculator beside you as you read.

points.heading: The four-step path from grams to grams
points.explanation:
Every mass-to-mass problem uses the same path: grams of what you have, then moles of what you have, then moles of what you want, then grams of what you want. Only the middle step uses the balanced equation. There you multiply by a mole ratio built from the coefficients, with moles on both the top and the bottom.

Example: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. How many grams of MgO form from 6.00 g Mg?
1. Grams to moles of Mg: 6.00 g ÷ 24.31 g/mol = 0.2468 mol Mg.
2. Moles of Mg to moles of MgO: 0.2468 mol Mg × (2 mol MgO / 2 mol Mg) = 0.2468 mol MgO.
3. Moles of MgO to grams: 0.2468 mol × 40.31 g/mol = 9.95 g MgO.

Sense check: the product (9.95 g) has more mass than the Mg (6.00 g) because MgO also contains oxygen. Keep extra digits in the middle steps and round only at the end.

points.heading: Finding the limiting reactant by comparing moles
points.explanation:
The limiting reactant is the one that runs out first. It decides how much product can form. To find it, compare the moles you have with the moles the reaction needs. Never compare grams.

Start with a hypothetical bicycle shop where 1 frame and 2 wheels make 1 bike. With 10 frames and 14 wheels, the 14 wheels make only 7 bikes. Wheels are limiting, and 3 frames are left over.

Now the same thinking with a reaction: 2Al + 3CuCl₂ → 2AlCl₃ + 3Cu, starting with 0.200 mol Al and 0.240 mol CuCl₂.
1. Ask how much CuCl₂ the Al would need: 0.200 mol Al × (3 mol CuCl₂ / 2 mol Al) = 0.300 mol CuCl₂.
2. Compare: 0.300 mol is needed, but only 0.240 mol is available.
3. The CuCl₂ runs out first, so CuCl₂ is the limiting reactant.

points.heading: Finding how much excess reactant is left
points.explanation:
The excess reactant is the one left over when the limiting reactant is gone. To find how much remains, follow the limiting reactant: work out the moles of the excess reactant it used, subtract them from the moles you started with, then convert the moles left to grams.

Continue the example above, where CuCl₂ is limiting (0.240 mol) and Al is in excess (0.200 mol at the start).
1. Moles of Al used: 0.240 mol CuCl₂ × (2 mol Al / 3 mol CuCl₂) = 0.160 mol Al.
2. Moles of Al left: 0.200 − 0.160 = 0.040 mol Al.
3. Grams of Al left: 0.040 mol × 26.98 g/mol = 1.08 g Al.

The order matters. You can only know how much of the excess reactant was used after you know which reactant is limiting.

points.heading: Why grams do not follow the coefficients
points.explanation:
Coefficients in a balanced equation compare moles, not grams. Substances have different molar masses, so a reactant with a smaller mass can still be the one in excess.

Example: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O, with 8.00 g CH₄ and 16.00 g O₂. The CH₄ has the smaller mass, but look at the moles.
- CH₄: 8.00 g ÷ 16.05 g/mol = 0.4984 mol.
- O₂: 16.00 g ÷ 32.00 g/mol = 0.5000 mol.

The CH₄ would need 2 × 0.4984 = 0.9969 mol O₂, and only 0.5000 mol is available. So O₂ is limiting and CH₄ is in excess.

The O₂ used 0.5000 × (1/2) = 0.2500 mol CH₄. That leaves 0.4984 − 0.2500 = 0.2484 mol CH₄, which is 0.2484 × 16.05 = 3.99 g. Always convert to moles first, then decide.

handouts.title: Mass-to-mass practice

blocks.text: Work both items alone. Write each of the four steps with its units. Use your periodic table for molar masses.
Item a
C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O
How many grams of CO₂ form from 22.0 g of C₃H₈?

blocks.hint: Show the four steps, with units.

blocks.text: Item b
2Al + 3CuCl₂ → 2AlCl₃ + 3Cu
How many grams of AlCl₃ form from 26.9 g of CuCl₂?

blocks.hint: Show the four steps, with units.

handouts.key:
Item a
The equation is balanced. M(C₃H₈) = 44.11 g/mol; M(CO₂) = 44.01 g/mol. Oxygen is assumed to be available in excess.
Four-step path: 22.0 g C₃H₈ → 0.49875 mol C₃H₈ → 1.49626 mol CO₂ → 65.9 g CO₂.
Working: 22.0 g C₃H₈ × (1 mol C₃H₈ / 44.11 g C₃H₈) = 0.49875 mol C₃H₈.
0.49875 mol C₃H₈ × (3 mol CO₂ / 1 mol C₃H₈) = 1.49626 mol CO₂.
1.49626 mol CO₂ × (44.01 g CO₂ / 1 mol CO₂) = 65.8504 g CO₂ ≈ 65.9 g CO₂.
Look for units that cancel and the 3:1 mole ratio. Common slips: applying the ratio directly to grams, reversing the ratio, or rounding too early.

Item b
The equation is balanced. M(CuCl₂) = 134.45 g/mol; M(AlCl₃) = 133.33 g/mol. Aluminum is assumed to be available in excess.
Four-step path: 26.9 g CuCl₂ → 0.200074 mol CuCl₂ → 0.133383 mol AlCl₃ → 17.8 g AlCl₃.
Working: 26.9 g CuCl₂ × (1 mol CuCl₂ / 134.45 g CuCl₂) = 0.200074 mol CuCl₂.
0.200074 mol CuCl₂ × (2 mol AlCl₃ / 3 mol CuCl₂) = 0.133383 mol AlCl₃.
0.133383 mol AlCl₃ × (133.33 g AlCl₃ / 1 mol AlCl₃) = 17.7839 g AlCl₃ ≈ 17.8 g AlCl₃.
Look for the 2:3 mole ratio and correct molar masses. Common slips: reversing the ratio or counting only one chlorine atom in a molar mass. Accept small differences from periodic-table rounding.

handouts.title: Limiting reactant and leftover mass

blocks.text: Work alone. Use your periodic table for molar masses.
2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO
A mixture has 12.0 g of Mg and 10.0 g of O₂.

items: Find the moles of Mg and the moles of O₂.
Name the limiting reactant.
Give the mass of the excess reactant left over.

blocks.hint: Moles of Mg and moles of O₂, with working and units.
Limiting reactant.
Mass of the excess reactant left, with working and units.

handouts.key:
Moles of Mg and moles of O₂
M(Mg) = 24.31 g/mol; M(O₂) = 32.00 g/mol.
n(Mg) = 12.0 g ÷ 24.31 g/mol = 0.493624 mol ≈ 0.494 mol.
n(O₂) = 10.0 g ÷ 32.00 g/mol = 0.3125 mol ≈ 0.313 mol.
Look for both conversions with units. Common slip: using 16.00 g/mol for O₂.

Limiting reactant
Mg is limiting. The available Mg needs 0.493624 mol Mg × (1 mol O₂ / 2 mol Mg) = 0.246812 mol O₂. This is less than the 0.3125 mol O₂ available, so oxygen is in excess.
Look for a comparison based on the balanced equation. Common slips: comparing grams directly or treating the required mole ratio as 1:1.

Mass of the excess reactant left
O₂ left = 0.3125 − 0.246812 = 0.065688 mol.
Mass left = 0.065688 mol × 32.00 g/mol = 2.10202 g ≈ 2.10 g O₂.
Look for subtraction of oxygen used from oxygen available, followed by conversion to grams. Common slips: subtracting the masses of different reactants or using all the available oxygen as the amount consumed.

handouts.title: Find and fix the mistake

blocks.text: The student below is hypothetical. Read the work, find what went wrong, then solve the problem correctly yourself.
Problem: In 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, a mixture has 6.0 g of H₂ and 32.0 g of O₂. Which reactant is limiting, and what mass of the excess reactant is left?
The student's work

items: 6.0 g of H₂ is less than 32.0 g of O₂, so H₂ is limiting.
O₂ left over = 32.0 g − 6.0 g = 26.0 g.

blocks.hint: What went wrong? Name the first step that is wrong and say why.
Redo the problem: find the moles of H₂ and of O₂, with working and units.
Limiting reactant, with a reason.
Mass of the excess reactant left, with working and units.

handouts.key:
What went wrong?
The first line is wrong. A smaller mass does not identify the limiting reactant. Convert each mass to moles and compare the amounts using the balanced equation. The second line also subtracts masses of different substances; leftover oxygen cannot be found by subtracting the starting mass of hydrogen.
Look for identification of the first line and an explanation involving moles and the required 2:1 ratio of H₂ to O₂.

Moles of H₂ and of O₂
M(H₂) = 2.02 g/mol; M(O₂) = 32.00 g/mol.
n(H₂) = 6.0 g ÷ 2.02 g/mol = 2.97030 mol.
n(O₂) = 32.0 g ÷ 32.00 g/mol = 1.00 mol.
Keep extra digits for the remaining calculations. Common slip: using atomic molar masses instead of molecular molar masses.

Limiting reactant, with a reason
O₂ is limiting. The 1.00 mol O₂ needs 2.00 mol H₂, and 2.97030 mol H₂ is available. Hydrogen is in excess.
Look for a comparison of moles available with moles needed. Common slip: comparing the two mole amounts without using the 2:1 ratio.

Mass of the excess reactant left
H₂ used = 1.00 mol O₂ × (2 mol H₂ / 1 mol O₂) = 2.00 mol H₂.
H₂ left = 2.97030 − 2.00 = 0.97030 mol.
Mass left = 0.97030 mol × 2.02 g/mol = 1.96 g H₂, or 2.0 g when rounded to the precision of the starting hydrogen mass.
Look for subtraction within the same substance and a final mass labeled H₂. Common slips: reporting oxygen as left over or subtracting 32.0 g from 6.0 g.

study.overview: Percent yield compares what a reaction actually gave you with the most it could have given. This guide covers how to calculate it, why it usually comes out below 100%, how to work backward from a wanted amount of product to the reactant you need, and the single path that solves every problem in the unit. Use it to prepare for the unit test, which is taken in class next time.

points.heading: Theoretical, actual and percent yield
points.explanation:
The theoretical yield is the most product the balanced equation allows. You calculate it from the limiting reactant: grams → moles → moles of product (mole ratio) → grams. The actual yield is the mass of product you really collect. You measure it on a balance, so you never calculate it.

Percent yield = actual yield ÷ theoretical yield × 100%. It works like a free-throw record: a player who makes 16 of 20 shots scores 16 ÷ 20 × 100% = 80%. For a reaction, the shots made are what you got and the shots taken are what was possible.

Example: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. A student heats 25.0 g of CaCO₃ and collects 10.5 g of CaO.
1. 25.0 g ÷ 100.09 g/mol = 0.2498 mol CaCO₃.
2. The ratio is 1:1, so 0.2498 mol CaO can form.
3. 0.2498 mol × 56.08 g/mol = 14.0 g CaO. This is the theoretical yield.
4. Percent yield = 10.5 ÷ 14.0 × 100% = 75.0%.

The 10.5 g is the actual yield. It is not the theoretical yield, and it goes on top of the fraction.

points.heading: Why the actual yield is usually lower
points.explanation:
Real reactions rarely recover every gram the equation allows. Three common causes:
• The reaction does not go fully to products. It may stop early or run backward.
• Side reactions use up some of the reactant to make something else.
• Product is lost when it is collected and transferred. It can stick to glassware or stay on filter paper.

Impure reactants also cut the amount of product. In the CaO example, 14.0 g was possible and 10.5 g was collected. Some CaCO₃ may not have decomposed, or some CaO may have been left behind in the container. Either one explains the 3.5 g gap.

A percent yield above 100% is a warning sign. It usually means the product was wet or impure, so the measured mass was too high.

points.heading: Working backward: how much reactant to start with
points.explanation:
Sometimes you know how much product you want and the percent yield, and you must find the reactant. A yield below 100% means you must start with more reactant than a perfect reaction would need. So the answer should come out larger than the perfect-yield answer. Divide by the percent yield written as a decimal.

Example: NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O, with HCl in excess. A student wants 10.0 g of NaCl and the percent yield is 85.0%.
1. Mass of NaCl needed in theory: 10.0 g ÷ 0.850 = 11.76 g.
2. Moles of NaCl: 11.76 g ÷ 58.44 g/mol = 0.2013 mol.
3. The ratio is 1:1, so 0.2013 mol NaOH is needed.
4. Mass of NaOH: 0.2013 mol × 40.00 g/mol = 8.05 g.

Check: a perfect yield would need only 10.0 g ÷ 58.44 g/mol × 40.00 g/mol = 6.84 g. Since 8.05 g is larger, the direction makes sense.

points.heading: One path for every problem
points.explanation:
Every problem in the unit uses the same path:
1. Work in moles. Convert grams to moles first.
2. Use the balanced equation only for the mole ratio.
3. If two amounts are given, find the limiting reactant. Compare the moles you have with the moles the ratio requires.
4. Decide which way yield goes. To find the actual yield, convert theoretical product into actual product. To find the theoretical yield, convert actual product into theoretical product.

Example: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂. A student mixes 10.0 g of Zn with 10.0 g of HCl and collects 15.0 g of ZnCl₂.
• Moles: 10.0 g ÷ 65.38 g/mol = 0.1530 mol Zn. 10.0 g ÷ 36.46 g/mol = 0.2743 mol HCl.
• Zn would need 2 × 0.1530 = 0.3059 mol HCl, but only 0.2743 mol is present. HCl is limiting.
• 0.2743 mol HCl × (1 mol ZnCl₂ ÷ 2 mol HCl) = 0.1371 mol ZnCl₂. At 136.29 g/mol this is 18.7 g, the theoretical yield.
• Percent yield = 15.0 ÷ 18.69 × 100% = 80.3%.
• Zn used = 0.1371 mol, so 0.1530 − 0.1371 = 0.0159 mol Zn is left. That is about 1.03 g.

Keep extra digits until the last step, then round once. Before you calculate, name the path you will follow.

handouts.key:
Item a
Theoretical yield of O₂: 15.0 g KClO₃ × (1 mol KClO₃ ÷ 122.55 g KClO₃) × (3 mol O₂ ÷ 2 mol KClO₃) × (32.00 g O₂ ÷ 1 mol O₂) = 5.88 g O₂.

Look for the 3:2 mole ratio. Common slip: using a 1:1 ratio or applying the coefficients directly to masses.

Item b
Theoretical yield of O₂: 5.00 g H₂O₂ × (1 mol H₂O₂ ÷ 34.02 g H₂O₂) × (1 mol O₂ ÷ 2 mol H₂O₂) × (32.00 g O₂ ÷ 1 mol O₂) = 2.35 g O₂.
Percent yield: (2.05 g ÷ 2.35156 g) × 100% = 87.2%.
Look for the 1:2 ratio of O₂ to H₂O₂. Common slips: reversing this ratio or dividing theoretical yield by actual yield. Percent yield has the unit %, not grams.

blocks.text: Read the problem. Answer the first question before you calculate anything. Then work the problem alone and show each step with units.
Problem

Sodium hydroxide reacts with an excess of hydrochloric acid: NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O. A student wants to make 10.0 g of NaCl. Suppose the percent yield is 85.0%. What mass of NaOH should the student start with?
Before you calculate
Should the mass of NaOH be larger or smaller than for a perfect yield? Say why.

blocks.hint: One or two sentences

blocks.text: Your work

blocks.hint: Show each step with units. Circle your answer.

blocks.text: Complete the sentence for your partner: I divided or multiplied by 0.850 because...

blocks.hint: Finish the sentence

handouts.key:
Before you calculate
The mass of NaOH must be larger than for a perfect yield. Only 85.0% of the theoretical amount of NaCl is collected, so more reactant is needed to collect 10.0 g.
Look for a clear connection between reduced yield and increased starting mass.

Your work
Required theoretical yield of NaCl = 10.0 g ÷ 0.850 = 11.7647 g.
Amount of NaCl = 11.7647 g ÷ 58.44 g/mol = 0.201313 mol.
NaOH and NaCl have a 1:1 mole ratio, so 0.201313 mol NaOH is needed.
Mass of NaOH = 0.201313 mol × 40.00 g/mol = 8.05 g NaOH. This is the answer to circle.
A perfect yield would require 10.0 g ÷ 58.44 g/mol × 40.00 g/mol = 6.84 g NaOH.

Partner sentence
Accept: I divided by 0.850 because 10.0 g is only 85.0% of the theoretical yield, and dividing finds the theoretical amount needed.
Common slip: multiplying 10.0 g by 0.850, which reduces the starting amount when it needs to increase.

handouts.key:
Item a
Path: moles of H₂O → mass of H₂O.
0.4999 mol H₂O × 18.02 g/mol = 9.008198 g = 9.008 g H₂O, to four significant figures.
Common slip: dividing by molar mass instead of multiplying.

Item b
Path: mass of Fe → moles of Fe → moles of FeCl₃ → mass of FeCl₃.
5.00 g Fe ÷ 55.85 g/mol = 0.0895255 mol Fe.
0.0895255 mol Fe × (2 mol FeCl₃ ÷ 2 mol Fe) = 0.0895255 mol FeCl₃.
0.0895255 mol FeCl₃ × 162.20 g/mol = 14.5 g FeCl₃.
Common slip: treating the coefficient 2 as a reason to double the product amount; the mole ratio is 2:2, or 1:1.

Item c: Limiting reactant and comparison
Amount of Zn = 10.0 g ÷ 65.38 g/mol = 0.152952 mol.
Amount of HCl = 10.0 g ÷ 36.46 g/mol = 0.274273 mol.
Reacting with all the Zn would require 2 × 0.152952 mol = 0.305904 mol HCl. Only 0.274273 mol HCl is available, so HCl is limiting.
Common slip: choosing the reactant with fewer moles without considering the 1:2 reaction ratio.

Item c: Theoretical yield
0.274273 mol HCl × (1 mol ZnCl₂ ÷ 2 mol HCl) = 0.137137 mol ZnCl₂.
0.137137 mol ZnCl₂ × 136.28 g/mol = 18.6890 g = 18.7 g ZnCl₂.
Common slip: calculating theoretical yield from the excess Zn.

Item c: Percent yield
(15.0 g ÷ 18.6890 g) × 100% = 80.3%.
Common slip: using a rounded intermediate value too early or reversing actual and theoretical yield.

Item c: Excess reactant remaining
Zn consumed = 0.137137 mol × 65.38 g/mol = 8.96599 g.
Zn remaining = 10.0 g − 8.96599 g = 1.03 g Zn.
This assumes the limiting HCl reacts completely through the stated reaction. The collected product mass alone does not establish how much Zn reacted.
Common slip: using the actual collected ZnCl₂ to calculate Zn consumed, even though product may have been lost during collection.

After checking
Answers vary. Look for an identified item and a specific reason tied to the student's work. Example: Item c needs a second look because I compared reactant moles without using the coefficients. Accept a statement that no item needs another look if it explains the student's confidence using a specific calculation or method.

study.overview: A test shows what you can do on your own, so the habits you use on the paper matter as much as the chemistry you know. The Unit test is on what has been taught so far, it is marked in points, and it counts for 50% of the course grade. This guide covers four habits: show every step, choose your path before you calculate, write units on every number, and keep extra digits until the last step. One calculation, turning grams of calcium carbonate into grams of calcium oxide, is worked in full below. The Problem sets set today count toward Problem sets, 20% of the course grade. Next time you react baking soda with vinegar, find the mass of carbon dioxide released from the mass lost, and compare it with a prediction. The same habits will carry into that lab.

points.heading: Work alone and show every step
points.explanation: On a test, the paper is the only evidence of what you can do. A bare number cannot be read, and a wrong bare number cannot be understood at all. Write each step on its own line so that someone reading it can follow your thinking. Example: finding the molar mass of K₂SO₄. Write the atom count first: 2 K, 1 S, 4 O. Then write 2(39.10) + 1(32.07) + 4(16.00). Then add: 78.20 + 32.07 + 64.00 = 174.27 g/mol. If you slip in the addition, the counting and the setup are still on the page. Check your work before you stop. Reread each line and ask whether the next line follows from it.

points.heading: Choose the path before you calculate
points.explanation: Most stoichiometry questions need a chain of conversions, and the common error is jumping into the arithmetic without a plan. First decide what you are given and what you must find. Then write the path in words and arrows. Example: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ is balanced as written. Suppose 25.0 g of CaCO₃ is heated. What mass of CaO forms? Path: g CaCO₃ → mol CaCO₃ → mol CaO → g CaO. The mole ratio is 1 mol CaO / 1 mol CaCO₃, because both have a coefficient of 1. Then follow the path: 25.0 g ÷ 100.09 g/mol = 0.24977 mol CaCO₃. Next, 0.24977 mol CaCO₃ × (1 mol CaO / 1 mol CaCO₃) = 0.24977 mol CaO. Finally, 0.24977 mol × 56.08 g/mol = 14.007 g, which rounds to 14.0 g CaO. The mole ratio always comes from the balanced equation, and it always sits in the middle of the path.

points.heading: Write units on every number
points.explanation: Units tell you whether a step makes sense. Grams divided by grams per mole leaves moles, so the unit cancels the way you want. Grams multiplied by grams per mole leaves g²/mol, which means you used the wrong operation. Example: in the CaCO₃ calculation, 25.0 g ÷ 100.09 g/mol gives mol because the grams cancel. Writing 25.0 g × 100.09 g/mol would give an odd unit, and that odd unit is your signal to stop and fix the step. A mole ratio needs units too: 1 mol CaO / 1 mol CaCO₃. The unit on top is the one you want and the unit on the bottom is the one you cancel. A final answer with no unit is incomplete.

points.heading: Keep extra digits, then round and check
points.explanation: Rounding in the middle of a problem shifts the last digits of your answer. Carry at least one or two extra digits through every step. Round once, at the end, to the number of significant figures the data allow. Example: in the CaCO₃ problem, 25.0 g has three significant figures. Keep 0.24977 mol through the middle and report 14.0 g at the end. Rounding to 0.25 mol early would give 14.02 g. That happens to round to the same answer here, but in a longer chain small early roundings can change the last digit. Then ask whether the answer is reasonable. CaO has a smaller molar mass than CaCO₃ and the mole ratio is 1 to 1, so the mass of CaO must be less than 25.0 g, and 14.0 g passes. Use the same check in next time’s lab. Before you start the calculations, decide what you will check, such as whether every mass you record has a unit.

segments.title: Where does the mass go?
segments.description:
Tell students that Problem sets: Unit test on stoichiometry is due now.
Put the question on the screen. Each student writes a letter and a one-line reason, then compares with a partner for one minute.
Hear two answers and ask where the mass could have gone.
segments.teacherNotes: Answer: C. The CO₂ gas escapes into the air, so the mass is not destroyed. In a sealed bottle the reading would stay at 130.00 g. Misconception: the mass vanished or the law of conservation of mass failed.

The baking soda is poured into the vinegar, the mixture fizzes until it stops, and the beaker and empty boat go back on the balance. The container is open to the air. The new reading is:
A. More than 130.00 g
B. Exactly 130.00 g
C. Less than 130.00 g
D. Impossible to tell

segments.title: Predicting the CO₂ from the baking soda
segments.description:
Put the balanced equation on the screen. Students write the mole ratio of CO₂ to NaHCO₃ and tell a partner what it is.
Explain that 75 mL of vinegar holds more acid than the baking soda used today, so the baking soda is the limiting reactant.
Students write the four-step path with units for 1.50 g of NaHCO₃, then the class works it on the board.
segments.teacherNotes: Work: 1.50 g ÷ 84.01 g/mol = 0.01786 mol NaHCO₃. Ratio 1:1 gives 0.01786 mol CO₂. × 44.01 g/mol = 0.786 g. Keep extra digits until the end. Check: 75 mL of 5% vinegar holds about 0.063 mol acid.
shown: NaHCO₃ + CH₃COOH → CH₃COONa + H₂O + CO₂
Suppose a pair weighs 1.50 g of baking soda. Predict the mass of CO₂ released.
Steps: grams NaHCO₃ → moles NaHCO₃ → moles CO₂ → grams CO₂

segments.title: The method and the safety rules
segments.description:
Give out the sheet “Baking soda and vinegar data sheet”. It holds the data table for two trials and space for the predicted CO₂ and the mass lost.
Show the steps on the screen and explain each one.
Students number the steps on their sheet and tell a partner who does which job in trial 1. They swap jobs for trial 2.
segments.teacherNotes:
Setup per pair: balance reading to 0.01 g, 250 mL beaker, 150 mL of 5% acidity vinegar, with a graduated cylinder to measure a fresh 75 mL portion for each trial, weighing boat, spoon. Trial 1 uses about 2 g of baking soda, trial 2 about 3 g. Record exact masses, not the targets.
Safety: before pairs start, check goggles, apron and closed-toe shoes. A student without them observes and writes up the data from a partner. No food or drink in the lab; nothing is tasted. Vinegar irritates eyes: immediately rinse a splash at the eyewash continuously for at least 15 minutes and alert the teacher.
shown: Steps: tare the boat and weigh about 2 g of baking soda, record the exact mass → pour 75 mL of vinegar into the beaker → put beaker and boat with baking soda on the balance, record the initial mass → add the baking soda in small portions, swirling gently → when fizzing stops, tap the boat clean, put beaker and empty boat on the balance, record the final mass

segments.title: Find and fix the plan
segments.description:
Put a hypothetical lab partner’s plan on the screen. Each student writes in one sentence what went wrong, writes the corrected first reading, and calculates the corrected mass lost.
Partners compare for one minute.
Hear two explanations and the corrected answer.
segments.teacherNotes: Error: the first reading left out the 1.20 g of baking soda. Correct initial: 121.30 + 1.20 = 122.50 g. Mass lost: 122.50 − 121.87 = 0.63 g. Prediction: 1.20 ÷ 84.01 × 44.01 = 0.629 g, so they agree. Say the partner is hypothetical.
shown: A hypothetical lab partner plans: weigh the beaker with the vinegar (121.30 g). Pour in 1.20 g of baking soda. When the fizzing stops, weigh the beaker again (121.87 g). Subtract: 121.30 − 121.87 = −0.57 g.
The partner says: “The mass lost is −0.57 g, so the CO₂ weighs less than nothing.”

segments.title: Lab: baking soda and vinegar
segments.description:
Pairs follow the steps on the data sheet for trial 1 with about 2 g of baking soda, recording the exact masses the balance shows.
Before any baking soda goes into the vinegar, each student calculates the predicted CO₂ in the space on the sheet.
After the final mass, they calculate the mass lost, empty and dry the beaker and boat, measure a fresh 75 mL of vinegar, and repeat for trial 2 with about 3 g, swapping jobs.
Both partners record every reading on their own data sheet.
segments.teacherNotes:
Example predictions: 2.00 g ÷ 84.01 g/mol × 44.01 g/mol = 1.05 g CO₂; 3.00 g gives 1.57 g. Mass lost = initial − final. Add baking soda in small portions so the foam does not overflow. Wait until bubbling stops before the final reading. A pair running behind may borrow a partner pair's second-trial readings. Students without gear observe and write up the data from a partner.
Safety: wipe spills at once; keep liquid away from the balance. Keep goggles on until all benches are clear.

segments.title: Clean up
segments.description:
Pairs pour the solution down the drain with running water and rinse the beaker, boat and cylinder.
They wipe the balance and bench, then wash their hands.
segments.teacherNotes: Safety: the leftover solution contains sodium acetate, water and excess acetic acid and can go down the drain with plenty of water. Goggles come off only after the bench is clear. Check that every pair keeps its data sheet.

segments.title: Measured against predicted
segments.description:
Each student takes the mass lost for trial 1 from the data sheet and finds the difference from the prediction.
They write one reason the two numbers might differ, in a few words.
Hear one pair, ask whether the mass lost was above or below the prediction, and write the reason on the board.
segments.teacherNotes: Pace: about 2 minutes to subtract, 1 to write, 1 to hear. Mass lost = initial − final. Difference = mass lost − predicted. Trial 2 is worked next time with the percent yield. Likely reasons: CO₂ stayed dissolved, spray or water vapor left with the gas, the reading was taken while still fizzing, balance rounding.

keyIdeas: In NaHCO₃ + CH₃COOH → CH₃COONa + H₂O + CO₂ every coefficient is 1, so 1 mol of baking soda makes 1 mol of CO₂ when the vinegar is in excess.
To predict the CO₂, follow the path grams NaHCO₃ → moles NaHCO₃ → moles CO₂ → grams CO₂, using 84.01 g/mol and 44.01 g/mol.
In an open container the CO₂ gas escapes into the air, so the balance reads less afterward. The mass lost is the mass of CO₂ released.

study.overview: In this lab you reacted baking soda with vinegar in an open beaker. You predicted the mass of CO₂ from the mass of baking soda, then measured the CO₂ by the mass the system lost. The reaction is NaHCO₃ + CH₃COOH → CH₃COONa + H₂O + CO₂. Every coefficient is 1, and the vinegar is in excess, so the baking soda is the limiting reactant. This guide covers the prediction, the reason the balance reading drops, how to take a correct first reading, and how to compare your measurement with the prediction. Keep your data sheet, because you will need your readings again.

points.heading: Predicting the CO₂ from the baking soda
points.explanation:
Because all coefficients are 1, 1 mol of NaHCO₃ makes 1 mol of CO₂ when the vinegar is in excess. To predict a mass, follow the path grams NaHCO₃ → moles NaHCO₃ → moles CO₂ → grams CO₂. Use 84.01 g/mol for NaHCO₃ and 44.01 g/mol for CO₂. Keep extra digits until the last step, then round.

Example: a pair weighs 1.50 g of baking soda.
1.50 g ÷ 84.01 g/mol = 0.01786 mol NaHCO₃.
The 1:1 ratio gives 0.01786 mol CO₂.
0.01786 mol × 44.01 g/mol = 0.786 g CO₂.

The same steps give 1.05 g of CO₂ for 2.00 g of baking soda and 1.57 g for 3.00 g. Write the units at every step. They show you whether you divided or multiplied by the right molar mass.

points.heading: Why the balance reads less afterward
points.explanation:
In an open container the CO₂ gas escapes into the air, so the balance reads less after the reaction. The mass is not destroyed. It leaves the beaker as gas. The mass lost, initial mass − final mass, is therefore the mass of CO₂ released. In a sealed bottle the gas could not leave, and the reading would stay the same.

Example: a beaker, vinegar, boat and baking soda together read 130.00 g. The baking soda is poured in, the fizzing stops, and the beaker and empty boat go back on the balance in the open air. The new reading is less than 130.00 g. The difference is the CO₂ that went into the air.

points.heading: Taking the first reading correctly
points.explanation:
The first reading must include everything that goes into the reaction: the beaker, the vinegar, and the boat with the baking soda. Then initial mass − final mass equals the CO₂ lost. If the baking soda is left out of the first reading, the subtraction gives a nonsense answer.

Example, a hypothetical lab partner: the beaker with vinegar reads 121.30 g. The partner pours in 1.20 g of baking soda, and after the fizzing stops the beaker reads 121.87 g. Subtracting 121.30 − 121.87 gives −0.57 g, which would mean the CO₂ has negative mass. The mistake is that 121.30 g did not include the baking soda. The correct initial mass is 121.30 + 1.20 = 122.50 g. The mass lost is 122.50 − 121.87 = 0.63 g. The prediction is 1.20 ÷ 84.01 × 44.01 = 0.629 g, so the two agree. A negative mass lost is a signal to check what your first reading included.

points.heading: Comparing the measured value with the prediction
points.explanation:
A measured value and a prediction rarely match exactly. Find the difference as measured minus predicted, where the measured value is your mass lost. A negative answer means the measurement is below the prediction. A positive answer means it is above. Then think about why the difference exists.

Likely reasons include CO₂ that stayed dissolved in the liquid, spray or water vapor that left with the gas, a final reading taken while the solution was still fizzing, and balance rounding. Name a cause and say which way it pushes the number. Dissolved CO₂ makes the mass lost too small. Spray leaving the beaker makes it too large.

Example: suppose a pair predicts 1.05 g of CO₂ and finds a mass lost of 1.01 g. The difference is 1.01 − 1.05 = −0.04 g, so the measurement is below the prediction. Some CO₂ staying dissolved in the solution would explain that direction.

Steps for each trial

items: Measure a fresh 75 mL of 5% vinegar in the graduated cylinder and pour it into the 250 mL beaker.

handouts.key:
Data table, in row order:

Mass of baking soda (g), Trial 1 and Trial 2: Each student's recorded mass must match the balance reading for that trial, to 0.01 g. Expect approximately 2 g and 3 g, respectively. Use the measured masses in calculations. Common slip: recording the target mass instead of the measured mass.

Initial mass: beaker, vinegar and boat with baking soda (g), Trial 1 and Trial 2: The combined balance reading before mixing, recorded to 0.01 g. It includes the baking soda and the weighing boat. Common slip: leaving out the baking soda's mass.

Final mass: beaker, solution and empty boat (g), Trial 1 and Trial 2: The combined balance reading after bubbling stops, recorded to 0.01 g. Include the empty boat. Common slips: leaving out the boat or weighing while the reaction is still bubbling.

Mass lost = initial − final (g), Trial 1: Subtract the recorded Trial 1 final mass from its initial mass. Report to 0.01 g.

Mass lost = initial − final (g), Trial 2: Subtract the recorded Trial 2 final mass from its initial mass. Report to 0.01 g. Common slip in either trial: reversing the subtraction. The mass lost estimates the mass of CO₂ released.

Predicted mass of CO₂, Trial 1: Use the exact measured mass of NaHCO₃. Show mass NaHCO₃ × (1 mol NaHCO₃ / 84.01 g NaHCO₃) × (1 mol CO₂ / 1 mol NaHCO₃) × (44.01 g CO₂ / 1 mol CO₂). The prediction is the measured baking soda mass multiplied by 0.523866…, in grams of CO₂. For a hypothetical measured mass of 2.00 g: 2.00 g ÷ 84.01 g/mol = 0.0238067 mol NaHCO₃; the 1:1 ratio gives 0.0238067 mol CO₂; multiplying by 44.01 g/mol gives 1.05 g CO₂.

Predicted mass of CO₂, Trial 2: Use the same calculation with the exact Trial 2 mass. For a hypothetical measured mass of 3.00 g: 3.00 g ÷ 84.01 g/mol = 0.0357100 mol NaHCO₃; the 1:1 ratio gives 0.0357100 mol CO₂; multiplying by 44.01 g/mol gives 1.57 g CO₂.

For both predictions, look for correct unit cancellation, the 1:1 mole ratio and a final answer in grams with appropriate significant figures. Keep extra digits until the final answer. Common slips: treating the mole ratio as a mass ratio, multiplying by 84.01 instead of dividing, or using the measured mass lost as the prediction.

keyIdeas: For the carbon dioxide lab, the theoretical yield is the CO₂ predicted from the baking soda, which is the limiting reactant. The actual yield is the mass lost, which is initial mass minus final mass. Percent yield = mass lost ÷ predicted CO₂ × 100%.
A percent yield far from 100% points to the method, not to a failure of the law of conservation of mass. A value above 100% means more mass left the beaker than the CO₂ can account for.

A source of error is a specific thing that happened in the procedure, and it has a direction. CO₂ that stays dissolved or is still fizzing makes the mass lost too small and the percent yield low. Spray and water vapor that leave with the gas make the mass lost too big and the percent yield high.

The results section reports the readings, one worked percent yield calculation with units, and the percent yield of each trial. The conclusion states the result, explains two sources of error and which way each pushes the result, and suggests one improvement. Every student writes it in their own words.

study.overview: Last time you predicted the mass of carbon dioxide from the baking soda in the baking soda and vinegar lab. Today you compared that prediction with the mass your balance showed was lost, and turned the two numbers into a percent yield. You then asked why a result might sit above or below 100%, and began drafting the results and conclusion of your lab report. This guide goes through the calculation, the sources of error and their directions, and what the two report sections need. The lab report counts toward Lab reports (30% of the course grade). Write it from your own data in your own words. You may share data with your partner, but not wording.

points.heading: Theoretical yield, actual yield and percent yield in this lab
points.explanation:
In this lab the vinegar is in excess, so the baking soda (NaHCO₃) is the limiting reactant. The CO₂ you predict from the baking soda is the theoretical yield. The actual yield is the mass lost: initial mass minus final mass. Percent yield = mass lost ÷ predicted CO₂ × 100%.

Worked example (a hypothetical pair, not your data). The reaction is NaHCO₃ + CH₃COOH → CH₃COONa + H₂O + CO₂. They used 2.40 g of baking soda. Molar masses: NaHCO₃ = 84.01 g/mol, CO₂ = 44.01 g/mol. Their initial mass was 142.60 g and their final mass was 141.55 g.

Step 1, predict the CO₂: grams NaHCO₃ → moles NaHCO₃ → moles CO₂ → grams CO₂. 2.40 g ÷ 84.01 g/mol = 0.02857 mol NaHCO₃. The mole ratio is 1:1, so 0.02857 mol CO₂. Then 0.02857 mol × 44.01 g/mol = 1.257 g CO₂. This is the theoretical yield.

Step 2, find the mass lost: 142.60 g − 141.55 g = 1.05 g. This is the actual yield.

Step 3, divide, then multiply by 100%: 1.05 g ÷ 1.257 g × 100% = 83.5%.

Two common slips are using the mass of baking soda as the theoretical yield, and flipping the fraction so the prediction sits on top. Keep the extra digits until the last step, then round to 0.1%. Put a unit on every number along the way.

points.heading: Sources of error: what happened and which way it pushes
points.explanation:
A source of error is a specific thing that happened in the procedure, and it pushes the result in one direction. “Human error” is not a source. Name what happened to the mass.

CO₂ that stays dissolved in the liquid, or a mixture that is still fizzing at the final reading, means less CO₂ has left the beaker. The mass lost is too small, so the percent yield is lower than it should be. Example (hypothetical): a pair predicted 1.40 g of CO₂ but measured a mass lost of 1.19 g because bubbles were still rising. Their percent yield is 1.19 ÷ 1.40 × 100% = 85.0%. Part of the CO₂ was still in the beaker.

Spray and water vapor that leave with the gas mean more than CO₂ left the beaker. The mass lost is too big, so the percent yield is higher than it should be. Example (hypothetical): a pair predicted 0.95 g of CO₂ but measured a mass lost of 1.05 g. Their percent yield is 1.05 ÷ 0.95 × 100% = 110.5%. More mass left the beaker than the CO₂ alone can account for.

A percent yield far from 100% points to the method. It does not mean the law of conservation of mass failed. The mass that seems to be missing went into the air, or it was still in the beaker. If your value is over 100% or very low, first recheck the arithmetic: initial minus final, and the molar masses 84.01 g/mol and 44.01 g/mol. If the arithmetic holds, ask which error source fits what you saw. The question that settles it is: what does this do to the mass lost?

points.heading: What the results and conclusion sections must hold
points.explanation:
The results section reports what you found. It holds your readings, one worked percent yield calculation with units, and the percent yield of each trial. Show the calculation once, in full, then list the values for both trials.

A results line might look like this, using made-up numbers: “Predicted CO₂ = 1.26 g; mass lost = 1.05 g; percent yield = 1.05 g ÷ 1.26 g × 100% = 83.3%.” Your numbers will be different, and every one needs a unit.

The conclusion explains what the results mean. It states your result and explains two sources of error. For each source, say what really happened in your lab, which way it pushed the mass lost, and which way it pushed the percent yield. Then suggest one improvement that would reduce one of the errors.

A good error explanation links three things: what happened, the effect on the mass lost, and the effect on the percent yield. For example: “Some CO₂ stayed dissolved, so the mass lost was too small and the percent yield was too low.” Only name an error that fits your own procedure and data.

Write both sections in your own words. When you read your partner’s draft, check that every number has a unit and that each explanation links the error to a higher or lower mass lost and percent yield. Do not copy any of their wording. Finish at home whatever you did not get written in class.

handouts.title: Which explanation fits?

blocks.text: The four cases below are made-up examples, not real class data. For each case, circle A or B. Then write a few words saying why. Ask yourself what your choice does to the mass lost.
Case 1
Pair A's percent yield was 112%. Which explanation fits?

items: A. Some of the CO₂ stayed dissolved in the liquid.
B. Some foam and liquid sprayed out of the beaker while it bubbled.

blocks.hint: Circle A or B, then write a few words saying why.

blocks.text: Case 2
Pair B's percent yield was 71%. Which explanation fits?

items: A. Some CO₂ was still in the beaker at the final reading.
B. Some liquid sprayed out of the beaker during the reaction.

blocks.hint: Circle A or B, then write a few words saying why.

blocks.text: Case 3
Pair C's percent yield was low. At their final reading, a few bubbles were still rising. Which fix should they use next time?

items: A. Wait until the bubbling stops before the final reading.
B. Add more vinegar to the beaker.

blocks.hint: Circle A or B, then write a few words saying why.

blocks.text: Case 4
Pair D's foam rose over the rim of the beaker and some of it spilled. Which fix should they use next time?

items: A. Add the baking soda in small portions.
B. Add all the baking soda at once.

blocks.hint: Circle A or B, then write a few words saying why.

handouts.key:
Case 1: B. Foam and liquid leaving the beaker add to the measured mass lost. Treating all that loss as CO₂ makes the apparent actual yield and percent yield too high. Common slip: choosing dissolved CO₂, which would lower the measured mass lost.

Case 2: A. CO₂ remaining in the beaker contributes to the final mass. The measured mass lost is too small, so the percent yield is too low. Common slip: choosing spilled liquid, which would increase the mass lost.

Case 3: A. Wait until bubbling stops before taking the final reading. Gas is still being released, so the current mass lost is too small. Waiting allows more CO₂ to escape and increases the measured mass lost toward the expected value. More vinegar is unnecessary when vinegar is already in excess. Common slip: assuming a low yield always means too little vinegar.

Case 4: A. Adding baking soda in small portions reduces foaming and spray. This helps prevent liquid loss from making the measured mass lost and percent yield too high. Common slip: saying the change produces more CO₂; its purpose is to prevent loss of liquid.

handouts.title: Draft: results and conclusion

blocks.text: Use the outline and the model sentences on the screen. Write from your own data, in your own words. You may read your partner's draft, but copy nothing from it. Finish at home anything you have not written.
Results

blocks.hint: Give your predicted CO₂, your mass lost and your percent yield for each trial. Show the calculation. Put a unit on every number.

blocks.text: Conclusion

blocks.hint: Name a source of error that really happened. Say whether it made your mass lost and your percent yield higher or lower.

blocks.text: Partner check (last two minutes)

items: Every number has a unit.
Each explanation connects the source of error to a higher or lower mass lost and a higher or lower percent yield.

handouts.key:
Results: Each student's values must match the partner pair's recorded data. For each trial, look for predicted CO₂ in g, mass lost in g, and percent yield in %. The worked calculation is percent yield = (mass lost ÷ predicted CO₂ mass) × 100%. Keep extra digits during calculation and round the final percent yield to 0.1%. If the prediction is shown, use moles of NaHCO₃ = baking soda mass ÷ 84.01 g/mol, the 1:1 NaHCO₃:CO₂ mole ratio, and predicted CO₂ mass = moles of CO₂ × 44.01 g/mol. Mass lost = initial mass − final mass. Common slips: reversing the yield fraction, using the baking soda mass as the predicted CO₂ mass, subtracting masses backward, or rounding too early.

Conclusion: Look for a specific source of error supported by the student's observations and a correct explanation of its direction. CO₂ remaining dissolved or taking the final reading while gas is still being released makes the final mass too high, the measured mass lost too low, and the percent yield too low. Foam, spray, or water vapor leaving the beaker adds to the mass lost and makes the apparent percent yield too high. Students should distinguish an observed event from a possible explanation. Common slips: writing only 'human error,' claiming an unobserved event happened, or naming an error without explaining its effect on both mass lost and percent yield.

Partner check: Masses carry g, molar masses carry g/mol, amounts of substance carry mol, and percent yields carry %. Trial labels and mole-ratio coefficients do not need units. Each error explanation must connect the event to the final mass, the measured mass lost, and the resulting higher or lower percent yield. Shared numerical data are appropriate; the draft wording must be the student's own.

segments.description:
Tell students that Lab reports: Lab: baking soda and vinegar, mass of carbon dioxide is due now, and that Problem sets: Analyzing the carbon dioxide data and writing the lab report is due now.

Hear two answers. Say that today’s lab uses this same equation.

shown: 2Al + 3CuCl₂ → 2AlCl₃ + 3Cu
How many moles of CuCl₂ react with 0.10 mol of Al? Write the mole ratio you used.

segments.title: Predict the limiting reactant
segments.description:
Put the equation, the molar masses and a hypothetical pair’s amounts on the screen. Each student writes which reactant they think will limit and why, in one line, then tells a partner.
Work the problem on the board: moles of each reactant, the moles of Al the CuCl₂ would need, then the comparison.
Show the steps on the screen. Students tell a partner what they would see in this beaker once the reaction stops, and one pair answers.

segments.title: The method and the safety rules
segments.description:
Give out the sheet “Copper chloride and aluminum data sheet”. Show the steps on the sheet and explain each one in about two minutes.
Check goggles, apron and closed-toe shoes in one minute. Pairs then number the steps on their sheet and agree who masses, who swirls and who records, in about two minutes.
segments.teacherNotes:
The sheet holds the amounts and values (2.50 g of CuCl₂ per cup, molar masses, the equation and mole ratio), the nine steps to number, a small table for the jobs, and the safety rules. Setup per pair: 150 mL beaker, cup with 2.50 g CuCl₂ in 50 mL water, foil piece, forceps, spoon, wash bottle, two labeled pre-massed watch glasses, paper towels, balance to 0.01 g. If the CuCl₂ is the dihydrate (170.48 g/mol), each cup holds 3.17 g CuCl₂·2H₂O, which equals 2.50 g of CuCl₂. The sheet says this, and students use 2.50 g with 134.45 g/mol, never 3.17 g.
Safety: CuCl₂ solution irritates eyes and skin and is harmful if swallowed; nothing is tasted. Rinse a skin splash with water. Rinse an eye splash at the eyewash for at least 15 minutes and alert the teacher. The reaction gives off heat and a little hydrogen gas, so keep flames out of the room and the room ventilated. Do not hold the warm beaker. Tie back long hair. A student without goggles, apron and closed-toe shoes observes and writes up the data from a partner. No food or drink.

segments.title: Lab: predict, then react
segments.description:
Each pair masses its strip of foil and records the exact mass in about two minutes. Each student then calculates the moles of Al and CuCl₂ and writes a prediction of the limiting reactant on the sheet in about three minutes.
Pairs add the foil to the CuCl₂ solution and swirl. They record color, bubbles and warmth every minute until the bubbling slows, about five minutes.
segments.teacherNotes:
Hand out foil strips of about 0.25 g to half the pairs and about 0.60 g to the rest; students record exact masses. Prediction check: CuCl₂ is 2.50 g ÷ 134.45 g/mol = 0.01859 mol and needs 0.01240 mol Al (0.334 g), using unrounded intermediate values. Fold each strip once, do not crumple it, so it stays in one piece and can be lifted out whole with forceps. Check each prediction before the foil goes in.
Safety: the beaker warms, so swirl by the rim only. Keep faces back from the beaker. Hands off the oven.

segments.title: Lab: collect the copper and leftover aluminum
segments.description:
When the bubbling has stopped, pairs pour off the liquid into the labeled waste container, keeping all solids in the beaker. They rinse the solids twice with a little water, swirling and letting the copper settle before pouring each rinse off.
With forceps they lift the leftover foil out whole. They hold it over the beaker and rub its surface with the back of the spoon under the wash bottle stream, so the copper coating falls into the beaker, until the foil looks silver with no brown coating. They pour off that rinse after the copper settles.
They use the spoon to transfer the copper to one pre-massed watch glass, then use small amounts of water to rinse all remaining copper from the beaker and spoon onto that same glass. They spread the copper thinly, place the clean foil on the other pre-massed watch glass, and carry both to the oven tray.
segments.teacherNotes:
Before class, pilot the separation with both starting amounts (about 0.25 g and 0.60 g of foil with 2.50 g CuCl₂). Confirm that the folded strip stays in one piece, that rubbing under the wash bottle leaves the foil silver, that the copper in the beaker holds no foil pieces, and that no copper is poured off with the rinses. Adjust the rubbing and settling steps and repeat both pilots. If either pilot still produces aluminum fragments or copper that cannot be removed from the aluminum, change the aluminum form or separation method and repeat both pilots before teaching the lab. Pairs with no foil left record that and still bring the empty glass.
The teacher puts the tray in a drying oven at about 100 °C for the rest of the lesson. Do not start until bubbling stops; use a wait to set out the glasses. Weighings made this lesson are first readings; they are repeated until constant (see the massing step).
Safety: pour all liquids and rinse water into the labeled copper waste container, never the drain. Only the teacher handles the hot oven and trays, with heat-resistant gloves. Avoid breathing in dry copper powder.

segments.title: Clean up
segments.description: Pairs rinse the beaker and spoon, pouring all rinse water into the labeled copper waste container. They wipe the balance and bench, then wash their hands.
segments.teacherNotes:
Check that every pair keeps its data sheet. Keep goggles on through the final weighing and sample cleanup.
Safety: the first rinse still holds copper, so it goes in the waste container, not the drain. Wash hands with soap even though gloves were not used.

segments.title: Find and fix the prediction
segments.description:
Give out the sheet “Find and fix the prediction”.
The sheet has a hypothetical lab partner’s prediction. Each student writes in a few words what went wrong, then calculates the moles of each reactant and names the true limiting reactant.
Partners compare for one minute. Hear one explanation and the corrected answer.
segments.teacherNotes: Say the partner is hypothetical. Pace: 1 minute to name the error, 4 to calculate, 1 to compare, 1 to hear. Error: Jordan compared grams, not moles. CuCl₂ is 3.00 ÷ 134.45 = 0.02231 mol; Al is 0.50 ÷ 26.98 = 0.01853 mol. CuCl₂ would use 0.01488 mol Al, so Al is in excess and CuCl₂ limits. At the end, the teacher takes the trays out of the oven so they cool.

segments.title: Mass the products and check the prediction
segments.description:
Give out the sheet “Copper chloride and aluminum data sheet: product masses”.
While the watch glasses cool for two minutes, each student writes in one sentence what their observations show was limiting and whether it matches their prediction.
Pairs then mass the copper glass and the foil glass and record both readings on the sheet, then subtract the mass written on each glass to find the solid alone. These are first readings; the glasses are dried again and massed once more next time.
segments.teacherNotes:
Pace: 2 minutes cooling and writing, 1 to mass and record, 1 to subtract. Use several balances. Handle glasses only after they are cool to the touch.
After class the teacher returns the labeled glasses to the oven or leaves them to air-dry. Next time pairs mass them again first thing. Wet copper may still read high now, so do not treat these first readings as final.
Reference values for 2.50 g CuCl₂: with 0.25 g foil, Al limits, no foil is left, and about 0.88 g Cu forms. With 0.60 g foil, CuCl₂ limits, about 0.27 g Al is left, and about 1.18 g Cu forms. These are theoretical reference masses. Hydrogen formation also consumes some aluminum, so the leftover aluminum may be below its prediction. Copper loss lowers the measured copper mass; retained water or mixed solids can raise it.

Set Lab reports and say it is due at the start of the class on Choosing a method for mixed stoichiometry problems. It counts toward Lab reports, 30% of the course grade.
Tell students to keep their data sheet. Next time they use their copper and aluminum masses to confirm the limiting reactant, calculate the percent yield of copper and draft the report.
Say that a short practice quiz on today’s lesson is for after class and counts toward no grade.

keyIdeas: In 2Al + 3CuCl₂ → 2AlCl₃ + 3Cu, the mole ratio of Al to CuCl₂ is 2 : 3. The limiting reactant is found by comparing moles, never grams.

To predict the limiting reactant, change both masses to moles. Then find the moles of Al that the CuCl₂ would use (moles CuCl₂ × 2/3) and compare with the moles of Al on hand. If less Al is available than the CuCl₂ requires, Al limits. If more Al is available than required, CuCl₂ limits.
The beaker gives evidence. If the blue-green color fades and foil is left, CuCl₂ was limiting. If the color stays and no foil is left, Al was limiting.
Copper and leftover aluminum must be rinsed and fully dry before weighing, because water left on them adds mass.
