study.overview: In this lab, aluminum foil reacts with copper chloride solution to make solid copper. Which reactant runs out first depends on how many moles of each you start with, not on how many grams. This guide covers the mole ratio, a method for predicting the limiting reactant, what the beaker shows, and how to mass the dry solids.

points.heading: Read the mole ratio from the balanced equation
points.explanation: The balanced equation is 2Al + 3CuCl₂ → 2AlCl₃ + 3Cu. The coefficients give the mole ratio of Al to CuCl₂, which is 2 : 3. To convert moles of one substance into moles of another, multiply by a ratio with the substance you want on top. Example: how many moles of CuCl₂ react with 0.10 mol of Al? Multiply 0.10 mol Al by 3 mol CuCl₂ / 2 mol Al to get 0.15 mol CuCl₂. A common mistake is turning the ratio upside down. That gives 0.067 mol, which is too small, because 3 mol of CuCl₂ are needed for every 2 mol of Al, so the CuCl₂ amount should be larger.

points.heading: Predict the limiting reactant by comparing moles, never grams
points.explanation: Follow these steps: change the grams of each reactant to moles, find the moles of Al that the CuCl₂ would use (moles CuCl₂ × 2/3), then compare with the moles of Al on hand. If less Al is on hand than needed, Al limits. If more Al is on hand than needed, CuCl₂ limits. Molar masses: Al 26.98 g/mol, CuCl₂ 134.45 g/mol, Cu 63.55 g/mol. Worked example: suppose a pair reacts 1.00 g of CuCl₂ with 0.10 g of aluminum foil. Moles of CuCl₂ = 1.00 ÷ 134.45 = 0.007438 mol. Moles of Al = 0.10 ÷ 26.98 = 0.003706 mol. The CuCl₂ would use 0.007438 × 2/3 = 0.004959 mol Al. That is more than the 0.003706 mol on hand, so Al limits. Why not compare grams? Because a gram of Al and a gram of CuCl₂ contain very different numbers of particles. In the lab, a cup holds 2.50 g of CuCl₂, which is 0.01859 mol and needs 0.01240 mol Al (0.334 g). A 0.60 g strip of foil is less massive than 2.50 g of CuCl₂, yet it holds 0.02224 mol Al, which is more than needed. So CuCl₂ limits. A 0.25 g strip holds only 0.009267 mol Al, so Al limits.

points.heading: Use the beaker as evidence
points.explanation: Your calculation is a prediction, and the beaker gives you a way to check it. If the blue-green color fades and a piece of foil is left, the CuCl₂ was used up first, so CuCl₂ was limiting. If the blue-green color stays and no foil is left, the Al was used up first, so Al was limiting. Example with 2.50 g of CuCl₂ and a 0.60 g strip: the calculation predicts that CuCl₂ limits, so you should see the color fade and some foil remain. About 0.27 g of Al is left, and about 1.18 g of Cu forms. With a 0.25 g strip, you should see no foil left and the color stay, with about 0.88 g of Cu formed. These are theoretical amounts. Your leftover aluminum may be lower than predicted, because some aluminum also reacts to make a little hydrogen gas. If your observations and your prediction disagree, check your mole calculation first, then think about what else could have used up aluminum.

points.heading: Rinse, dry and subtract to find the mass of each solid
points.explanation: Rinse the copper and the leftover aluminum, then dry them completely before you trust a mass. Water left on the solids adds mass, so wet copper reads too high. Each solid sits on a pre-massed watch glass with its mass written on it. The balance reads glass plus solid, so subtract the written mass of the glass to find the solid alone. Hypothetical example: a glass marked 41.20 g reads 41.95 g with copper on it. The copper alone is 41.95 − 41.20 = 0.75 g. Readings taken soon after the oven are first readings. The glasses are dried again and massed once more. A reading is final only when it stops changing. Other things also change the result. Copper poured off with a rinse lowers the measured copper mass. Water left on the solids, or copper mixed in with the aluminum, raises it.

handouts.title: Copper chloride and aluminum data sheet
handouts.usedIn: The method and the safety rules

blocks.text: Keep this sheet for the whole lab. Number the steps in order, then agree on who masses, who swirls and who records.
Amounts and values

items: Each cup holds 2.50 g of CuCl₂ in 50 mL of water. Use 2.50 g and 134.45 g/mol in every calculation.
If your cup is labeled CuCl₂·2H₂O, its 3.17 g of solid counts as 2.50 g of CuCl₂. Never use 3.17 g.
Molar masses: CuCl₂ 134.45 g/mol; Al 26.98 g/mol; Cu 63.55 g/mol.
Equation: 3CuCl₂ + 2Al → 3Cu + 2AlCl₃. The mole ratio of CuCl₂ to Al is 3 : 2.
Balance reads to 0.01 g.

blocks.text: Steps

rows: Mass your strip of foil and record the exact mass.
Calculate the moles of Al and CuCl₂. Write your prediction of the limiting reactant.
Fold the foil once (do not crumple it). Add it to the CuCl₂ solution in the 150 mL beaker and swirl by the rim.
Record color, bubbles and warmth every minute until the bubbling slows, about five minutes.
When the bubbling has stopped, pour the liquid into the labeled waste container. Keep all solids in the beaker.
Rinse the solids twice with a little water. Let the copper settle before pouring off each rinse.
Lift the leftover foil out whole with forceps. Rub it with the back of the spoon under the wash bottle stream over the beaker until it looks silver.
Use the spoon and small amounts of water to move all the copper onto one pre-massed watch glass. Put the foil on the other. Carry both to the oven tray.
After the glasses cool, mass each one. Subtract the mass of the glass to find the mass of the copper and of the aluminum.
blocks.caption: Write the step number in the first column.

blocks.text: Safety

items: Wear goggles, apron and closed-toe shoes. Tie back long hair. No food or drink.
CuCl₂ solution irritates eyes and skin and is harmful if swallowed. Taste nothing.
Skin splash: rinse with water. Eye splash: go to the eyewash for at least 15 minutes and tell the teacher.
The beaker warms and a little hydrogen gas forms. Swirl by the rim only, keep your face back, and keep flames out of the room.
All liquids and rinse water go in the labeled copper waste container, never the drain.
Only the teacher handles the oven and hot trays. Avoid breathing in dry copper powder.
Wash your hands with soap at the end.

blocks.text: Use the exact mass of your foil strip and 2.50 g of CuCl₂. Molar masses: CuCl₂ 134.45 g/mol, Al 26.98 g/mol. Equation: 3CuCl₂ + 2Al → 3Cu + 2AlCl₃.

My prediction: which reactant limits, and why.

blocks.caption: Observations, once a minute until the bubbling slows

handouts.key:
Mass of my foil strip: The pair’s actual balance reading in grams, recorded to 0.01 g. Use this measured value throughout.

Moles of Al: n(Al) = measured foil mass ÷ 26.98 g/mol. For a measured mass of 0.25 g: 0.00927 mol Al. For 0.60 g: 0.0222 mol Al.

Moles of CuCl₂: n(CuCl₂) = 2.50 g ÷ 134.45 g/mol = 0.0186 mol. Use the CuCl₂-equivalent mass, including when the cup is labeled CuCl₂·2H₂O.

Prediction: The CuCl₂ requires (2.50 ÷ 134.45) × 2/3 = 0.0124 mol Al, equivalent to 0.334 g Al. Below this foil mass, Al limits. Above it, CuCl₂ limits. At the exact stoichiometric amount, neither reactant is in excess in the ideal reaction. Thus, 0.25 g Al limits; with 0.60 g Al, CuCl₂ limits. Look for a comparison using the balanced equation. Common slips: comparing grams directly, reversing 2/3, or assuming equal moles react.

Observation table, rows 1 through 5: Each Color cell records the observed solution color and any reddish-brown copper. Each Bubbles and warmth cell records the observed bubbling and temperature change at that minute. Accept the pair’s actual observations; the rate and timing vary. Expected overall pattern: copper forms, bubbling occurs, and the beaker warms. With Al limiting, blue-green solution may remain and the foil may disappear. With CuCl₂ limiting, the solution’s blue-green color fades and foil remains. Look for observations rather than calculated or invented entries. Common slip: treating bubbles alone as proof of which reactant limits.

handouts.title: Find and fix the prediction

blocks.text: Jordan is a hypothetical lab partner. Jordan has 3.00 g of CuCl₂ and 0.50 g of Al. Jordan predicts: "Al will be the limiting reactant, because 0.50 g is less than 3.00 g." Equation: 3CuCl₂ + 2Al → 3Cu + 2AlCl₃. Molar masses: CuCl₂ 134.45 g/mol, Al 26.98 g/mol.

blocks.hint: In a few words, what went wrong?
Moles of CuCl₂ and moles of Al. Show your work.
Use the mole ratio to compare the two amounts. Name the true limiting reactant.

handouts.key:
What went wrong: Jordan compared masses directly. Different substances have different molar masses, and the reaction requires a 3 : 2 mole ratio.

Moles of CuCl₂: 3.00 g ÷ 134.45 g/mol = 0.02231 mol, or 0.0223 mol to three significant figures.

Moles of Al: 0.50 g ÷ 26.98 g/mol = 0.01853 mol, or 0.019 mol to two significant figures. Keep unrounded values during the comparison.

Mole-ratio comparison: The CuCl₂ needs (3.00 ÷ 134.45) × 2/3 = 0.01488 mol Al. This is less than the 0.01853 mol Al available, so CuCl₂ is the limiting reactant and Al is in excess. Accept the equivalent comparison: the Al would require 0.02780 mol CuCl₂, more than the 0.02231 mol available. Common slips: comparing grams, comparing moles without the coefficients, or reversing the mole ratio.

handouts.title: Copper chloride and aluminum data sheet: product masses
handouts.usedIn: Mass the products and check the prediction

blocks.text: These are first readings. The glasses are dried again and massed once more next time. Subtract the mass written on each glass from the reading.

blocks.hint: In one sentence: what do your observations show was limiting, and does it match your prediction?

handouts.key:
Observation sentence: Accept a conclusion tied to the pair’s observations and stating whether it agrees with the original prediction. Disappearance of foil with blue-green solution remaining supports Al limiting. Remaining silver foil with the blue-green color depleted supports CuCl₂ limiting. If observations are unclear, accept a qualified conclusion that identifies the uncertainty.

Copper glass, Glass + solid (g): The actual first balance reading for the cooled copper watch glass and its contents, recorded to 0.01 g.

Copper glass, Solid alone (g): Copper-glass reading − pre-massed empty copper-glass mass. The result is the first measured mass of the collected solid, in grams.

Foil glass, Glass + solid (g): The actual first balance reading for the cooled foil watch glass and its contents, recorded to 0.01 g. If no foil remains, record the empty glass reading.

Foil glass, Solid alone (g): Foil-glass reading − pre-massed empty foil-glass mass. If no foil remains, the result should be approximately 0.00 g within balance precision.

Common slips: reporting the glass-plus-solid reading as the solid mass, subtracting the wrong glass mass, or treating these first readings as final dry masses. Retained water can increase a first reading.

keyIdeas: Leftover aluminum is evidence of which reactant limited. If foil remains and the blue color has disappeared after the reaction finishes, the evidence supports Al being in excess and CuCl₂ running out first. To confirm it, find the Al used (starting mass − mass left) and compare it with the Al the CuCl₂ needed, using the 2 : 3 mole ratio.
A smaller mass does not make a reactant limiting. Compare moles, using 26.98 g/mol for Al and 134.45 g/mol for CuCl₂.

The theoretical yield of copper comes from the limiting reactant. In 2Al + 3CuCl₂ → 2AlCl₃ + 3Cu, 3 mol CuCl₂ make 3 mol Cu, so the ratio is 1 : 1. Convert moles of Cu to grams with 63.55 g/mol. The actual yield is the measured mass of dry copper. Percent yield = actual yield ÷ theoretical yield × 100%.

A data table lists every measured value with a label and a unit. The analysis section makes a claim, backs it with evidence and one worked calculation, and explains any gap from 100% with a cause and its direction.

study.overview: After the reaction, the aluminum foil that is left over tells you which reactant ran out. In this guide you will use that evidence to confirm the limiting reactant, find the percent yield of copper, and plan the data table and analysis sections of your lab report. All the numbers below come from one hypothetical pair of students, not from your class’s data. Their reaction is 2Al + 3CuCl₂ → 2AlCl₃ + 3Cu. The molar masses are Al 26.98 g/mol, CuCl₂ 134.45 g/mol and Cu 63.55 g/mol.

points.heading: Leftover aluminum shows which reactant limited
points.explanation:
If foil is still in the beaker and the blue color has gone after the reaction finishes, the evidence supports Al being in excess and CuCl₂ running out first. You can confirm this with numbers. Find the Al used (starting mass − mass left over). Then find the Al the CuCl₂ needed, using the 2 : 3 mole ratio. If the two agree within the balance’s precision, the claim is confirmed.

Example: the hypothetical pair started with 2.00 g of CuCl₂ and 1.02 g of Al foil. The CuCl₂ is 2.00 ÷ 134.45 = 0.01488 mol. Multiply by 2/3 to get 0.00992 mol Al, which is 0.00992 × 26.98 = 0.268 g of Al needed. So the predicted foil left over is 1.02 − 0.268 = 0.752 g. The pair measured 0.76 g left, so the Al used was 1.02 − 0.76 = 0.26 g. That matches the 0.268 g needed to within the balance’s 0.01 g, so CuCl₂ was the limiting reactant.

points.heading: Compare moles, not grams
points.explanation:
A smaller mass does not make a reactant limiting. Grams are not particles, and the two reactants have very different molar masses. Always convert both starting masses to moles, then use the mole ratio from the balanced equation.

Example: in the hypothetical pair, Al (1.02 g) has a smaller mass than CuCl₂ (2.00 g). Comparing grams would wrongly point to Al as the limiting reactant. In moles, Al is 1.02 ÷ 26.98 = 0.0378 mol. The CuCl₂ is only 0.01488 mol, and it needs just 0.00992 mol of Al. Al is in large excess, so CuCl₂ limits. The foil left over agrees with this. When your own result looks odd, check the first step where you might have compared grams.

points.heading: Theoretical yield, actual yield and percent yield
points.explanation:
The theoretical yield of copper always comes from the limiting reactant, never the excess one. In this equation 3 mol CuCl₂ make 3 mol Cu, so the ratio is 1 : 1. Convert moles of Cu to grams with 63.55 g/mol. The actual yield is the measured mass of dry copper: it is measured, not calculated. Then:

Percent yield = actual yield ÷ theoretical yield × 100%

Example: the hypothetical pair’s limiting reactant was 0.01488 mol CuCl₂. That makes 0.01488 mol Cu, and 0.01488 × 63.55 = 0.945 g of copper, the theoretical yield. They collected 0.83 g of dry copper. Their percent yield is 0.83 ÷ 0.945 × 100% = 87.8%. Two common slips are starting from the excess reactant and flipping the fraction. A value above 100% is a warning sign, since it can mean damp copper or bits of foil mixed in with it. Keep extra digits until the last step, then round the percent yield to 0.1%.

points.heading: Writing the data table and analysis sections
points.explanation:
The data table lists only measured values. Give each a label and a unit. For the hypothetical pair, rows would read: starting mass of CuCl₂, 2.00 g; starting mass of Al foil, 1.02 g; mass of Al foil left over, 0.76 g; mass of dry copper, 0.83 g.

The analysis section makes a claim, backs it with evidence, and shows one worked calculation. It also explains any gap from 100% with a cause and its direction. A model for the pair might read: “CuCl₂ was the limiting reactant, because 0.26 g of Al was used and 0.268 g was needed, and foil was left over. The percent yield of copper was 0.83 g ÷ 0.945 g × 100% = 87.8%. Copper lost while decanting or rinsing would make the yield lower.”

Write your own sentences from your own data. Shared data is fine, but shared wording is not. Before you finish, check that every number has a unit and that your percent yield uses the theoretical yield.

Mass of Al the CuCl₂ needed, with your working
The limiting reactant was ___ because ___.

handouts.key:
1. Mass of Al used = starting mass of Al foil − mass of Al foil left over, in g. Look for the student's measured masses and a correct subtraction. Common slip: reversing the subtraction.
2. Mass of Al needed = (starting mass of CuCl₂ ÷ 134.45 g/mol) × (2 mol Al/3 mol CuCl₂) × 26.98 g/mol. This equals 0.13378 × the starting mass of CuCl₂, in g. Look for the 2:3 mole ratio and units that cancel to grams of Al. Common slip: using 3:2.
3. Accept a claim supported by the student's readings and mole calculation. If clean Al remains and the starting Al exceeds the calculated requirement: 'The limiting reactant was CuCl₂ because aluminum remained after the reaction, and the starting aluminum exceeded the amount needed to react with the CuCl₂.' The measured Al used should approximately match the calculated requirement. If the starting Al is below the requirement and is consumed, Al limits. If the amounts are exactly stoichiometric, neither reactant is in excess. Common slip: calling the leftover reactant the limiting reactant.

handouts.key:
1. Mass of copper collected = mass of paper and copper − mass of paper, in g. Use the student's measured readings. Common slip: counting the paper as copper.
2. Calculate both possible copper yields when needed. From CuCl₂: (mass of CuCl₂ ÷ 134.45 g/mol) × (1 mol Cu/1 mol CuCl₂) × 63.55 g/mol. From Al: (starting mass of Al ÷ 26.98 g/mol) × (3 mol Cu/2 mol Al) × 63.55 g/mol. The smaller yield is the theoretical yield, in g Cu, and identifies the limiting reactant. Accept a calculation using the limiting reactant already established from the data. Common slip: calculating theoretical yield from the excess reactant.
3. Percent yield = (mass of copper collected ÷ theoretical mass of copper) × 100%. Both masses must use the same unit; they cancel, leaving a percentage. Keep extra digits during calculation and round the final result to 0.1%. A result above 100% can indicate wet copper or contamination; a low result can reflect copper lost during transfer or rinsing. Common slip: dividing theoretical yield by actual yield.

blocks.text: Suppose a pair of students, Pair C, ran the same reaction and collected the data below. These numbers are hypothetical. Read their reasoning, then find what is wrong and fix it.

blocks.label: Molar masses
blocks.value: CuCl₂ 134.45 g/mol; Al 26.98 g/mol; Cu 63.55 g/mol

rows: Mass of Al foil left over
blocks.caption: Pair C's data

blocks.text: Pair C's reasoning

items: We compared the starting masses. Al is 0.45 g and CuCl₂ is 2.50 g. Al has the smaller mass, so Al is the limiting reactant.
Theoretical yield from Al: 0.45 g ÷ 26.98 g/mol = 0.0167 mol Al; × 3 Cu/2 Al = 0.0250 mol Cu; × 63.55 g/mol = 1.59 g Cu.

blocks.hint: What is wrong with Pair C's work?
What is the correct limiting reactant?
What is the correct percent yield? Show your working and units.

handouts.key:
1. Pair C compared grams instead of using the balanced equation's mole ratio. A smaller starting mass does not establish the limiting reactant. Their calculation uses all the starting Al even though 0.12 g remains. Starting amounts: 2.50 g ÷ 134.45 g/mol = 0.0185943 mol CuCl₂; 0.45 g ÷ 26.98 g/mol = 0.0166790 mol Al. The CuCl₂ requires 0.0185943 × 2/3 = 0.0123962 mol Al, or 0.334449 g Al, which is less than the 0.45 g available.
2. CuCl₂ is the limiting reactant. The predicted leftover Al is 0.45 − 0.334449 = 0.115551 g, which rounds to 0.12 g and agrees with the measured leftover. Measured Al used = 0.45 − 0.12 = 0.33 g.
3. Theoretical copper yield = (2.50 g ÷ 134.45 g/mol) × (3 mol Cu/3 mol CuCl₂) × 63.55 g/mol = 1.181666 g Cu. Percent yield = (1.12 g ÷ 1.181666 g) × 100% = 94.8%. Look for the theoretical yield from CuCl₂ and the actual yield in the numerator. Common slip: retaining the theoretical yield calculated from excess Al.

keyIdeas: Every multi-step problem starts with the given and the wanted quantity. Write the conversion path with units before any number is worked.
The balanced equation is used for one step only, the mole ratio. Grams are never compared or converted with the coefficients.

When two amounts are given, find the limiting reactant by comparing moles. Then continue from it, either by comparing moles needed with moles available or by running each reactant to grams of product and taking the smaller.
A yield step has a direction. Theoretical yield comes from the path, and percent yield = actual yield ÷ theoretical yield × 100%.

vocabulary.definition: The amount a problem tells you, such as 5.00 g of H₂. It is where the path starts.
The amount a problem asks you to find, such as grams of NH₃. It is where the path ends.
The ordered steps from the given quantity to the wanted quantity, such as grams → moles → moles → grams, written with units before calculating.
A quick test of an answer before you trust it, such as making the units cancel, estimating with rounded numbers, or comparing with the total mass of the reactants.
A rough answer found by rounding each number to an easy one, such as 5 g ÷ 2 g/mol × 2/3 × 17 g/mol ≈ 28 g.

study.overview: Multi-step stoichiometry problems are easier when you plan before you calculate. Name what is given and what is wanted, write the conversion path with units, and use the balanced equation for one step only: the mole ratio. If two amounts are given, find the limiting reactant first. A yield step goes in a set direction. Then check every answer before you trust it.

points.heading: Write the path with units first, and use the equation once
points.explanation:
Start with the given quantity and the wanted quantity. Write the steps with units and no numbers. The balanced equation is used for one step only, the mole ratio between moles of one substance and moles of another. Grams always go through molar mass first. The coefficients do not compare grams. In N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, the 3 and 2 do not mean 3 g of H₂ for 2 g of NH₃.

Example: how many grams of NH₃ can form from 5.00 g of H₂ with plenty of N₂? Path: grams H₂ → moles H₂ → moles NH₃ → grams NH₃. Work: 5.00 g ÷ 2.016 g/mol = 2.480 mol H₂. Multiply by 2/3 to get 1.653 mol NH₃. Multiply by 17.03 g/mol to get 28.2 g NH₃. “Plenty of N₂” tells you H₂ is the limiting reactant, so you start from H₂.

points.heading: With two amounts given, compare moles to find the limiting reactant
points.explanation:
Do not decide by comparing grams. Change both masses to moles, then use the mole ratio. There are two reliable ways to finish. Way A: compare the moles needed with the moles available to find the limiting reactant, then continue from it only. Way B: run each reactant to grams of product and take the smaller answer as the theoretical yield.

Example: a reactor holds 14.0 g of N₂ and 4.00 g of H₂ (N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃). Moles: 14.0 ÷ 28.02 = 0.4996 mol N₂, and 4.00 ÷ 2.016 = 1.984 mol H₂. Way A: 0.4996 mol N₂ needs 3 × 0.4996 = 1.499 mol H₂. There is 1.984 mol, so H₂ is in excess and N₂ limits. Then 0.4996 mol N₂ gives 0.9993 mol NH₃, which is 17.0 g. Way B: H₂ alone could make 22.5 g and N₂ alone could make 17.0 g. The smaller, 17.0 g, is the theoretical yield. Notice that H₂ has the smaller mass (4.00 g) but is not the limiting reactant. This is why you compare moles, not grams.

points.heading: A yield step has a direction
points.explanation:
Theoretical yield is what the path predicts from the limiting reactant. Actual yield is what you measure. Percent yield = actual yield ÷ theoretical yield × 100%. Always find the theoretical yield first, and put it in the denominator.

Example: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. A student burns 5.00 g of Mg in 4.00 g of O₂ and collects 7.60 g of MgO. Moles: 5.00 ÷ 24.31 = 0.2057 mol Mg, and 4.00 ÷ 32.00 = 0.1250 mol O₂. Mg needs only 0.1028 mol O₂, so Mg limits. Theoretical yield: 0.2057 mol MgO × 40.30 g/mol = 8.29 g. Percent yield: 7.60 ÷ 8.29 × 100% = 91.7%.

Sometimes the direction is reversed. If you want a certain actual mass and know the percent yield, divide the wanted mass by (percent yield ÷ 100) to get the theoretical yield. Then run the path backward to find the starting mass. Suppose you want 10.0 g of product at an 80% yield. The theoretical yield must be 10.0 ÷ 0.80 = 12.5 g.

points.heading: Check every answer with units, an estimate and total mass
points.explanation:
Three quick checks catch most errors. First, make the units cancel so that only the wanted unit is left. Second, round the numbers and estimate. Third, compare the product mass with the total mass of the reactants. A product cannot weigh more than everything that went in. A calculator showing many digits does not mean the answer is right.

Example: a student says 2.00 g of H₂ with plenty of N₂ gives 16.9 g of NH₃. Estimate: 2 g ÷ 2 g/mol = 1 mol H₂. Multiply by 2/3 to get about 0.67 mol NH₃. Multiply by 17 g/mol to get about 11 g. The claim is not reasonable, because the student skipped the 2/3 mole ratio. The correct answer is 11.3 g. The total-mass check agrees: 2.00 g of H₂ needs 9.27 g of N₂, so the product cannot exceed 11.3 g.

The total-mass check also works in simpler cases. If 10.0 g of Mg burns in oxygen, the MgO must weigh more than 10.0 g, because oxygen joins the magnesium. A claim of 6.2 g of MgO fails at once.
